step: Apply for autorisation de séjour et de travail (third-country nationals)
authority: Direction de l'Immigration (Ministère des Affaires étrangères et européennes)
form_name: Application for autorisation de séjour — salarié
field_label: Salary threshold; employment contract; employer matricule
deadline_label: At least 3 months before intended start date
non_obvious_official_guidance: The third-country national applies for a combined residence and work authorisation via MyGuichet.lu before entering Luxembourg for work.
non_obvious_actual_reality: In practice the employer must initiate and submit the application, not the employee. The employee cannot legally start work until the authorisation is granted; processing takes 6–12 weeks. Rush travel plans have caused compliance failures.
non_obvious_action_required: Employer submits via MyGuichet.lu at least 90 days before the desired start date and tracks status actively. Employee must not travel to Luxembourg for work before receiving the authorisation or a visa D.
source: guichet.lu — Autorisation de séjour: salarié (ressortissant pays tiers)

step: Apply for EU Blue Card (carte bleue européenne) — highly qualified third-country national
field_label: Gross annual salary ≥ 1.5× Luxembourg average wage; recognised higher-education qualification
deadline_label: At least 3 months before intended start date
non_obvious_official_guidance: EU Blue Card is available to highly qualified non-EU workers with a recognised higher-education qualification and a job offer meeting the salary threshold.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Luxembourg's Blue Card salary threshold is adjusted annually and frequently misquoted; a lower threshold applies for shortage occupations. Degree equivalency from non-EU universities is not automatic and must be assessed separately before submission.
non_obvious_action_required: Verify the current salary threshold on guichet.lu before the offer letter is signed. Initiate degree-equivalency assessment early if the qualification is from outside the EU.
source: guichet.lu — Carte bleue européenne

step: Confirm EU/EEA/Swiss right to work — no prior authorisation required
field_label: Valid national identity card or passport
deadline_label: Before start date
non_obvious_official_guidance: EU/EEA/Swiss nationals may live and work in Luxembourg without a work permit or prior authorisation.
non_obvious_actual_reality: No advance permission is needed, but the employee must still register at the commune within 3 days of arrival. Employers sometimes incorrectly request additional work authorisation from EU employees — this is not legally required and creates unnecessary delay.
non_obvious_action_required: Employee carries a valid national ID or passport. Employer does not file any work-permit application for EU/EEA/Swiss nationals. Employee registers at the commune immediately on arrival.
source: guichet.lu — Citoyens UE/EEE/CH: séjour et travail au Luxembourg

step: Obtain recognition of professional qualifications for regulated professions
authority: Ministère de l'Éducation nationale / sectoral authorities (Ordre des médecins, Barreau, etc.)
form_name: Application for recognition of professional qualifications
field_label: Diploma; professional licence; work-experience evidence
deadline_label: At least 90 days before start date — recognition can take 3–6 months
non_obvious_official_guidance: EU Directive 2005/36/EC provides automatic recognition for certain regulated professions (doctors, nurses, dentists, pharmacists, vets, architects). Other regulated professions require a formal application.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Partial qualifications or non-standard specialisations may not qualify for automatic recognition even within the EU. Most corporate and office roles are unregulated — HR teams often apply unnecessarily, wasting weeks.
non_obvious_action_required: Check whether the specific role appears on Luxembourg's regulated-professions list before starting any recognition application. For regulated roles, submit the full dossier at least 90 days pre-start.
source: guichet.lu — Reconnaissance des qualifications professionnelles

step: File déclaration d'arrivée at the commune (municipality) of residence
field_label: Proof of address (lease or employer letter); passport/ID; employment contract; passport photos
deadline_label: Within 3 days of taking up residence
non_obvious_official_guidance: Any person taking up residence in Luxembourg must declare their arrival at the administration of their commune of residence within 3 days.
non_obvious_actual_reality: The 3-day window is strict in law but commune offices are often closed Mondays and have limited appointment slots. The commune declaration triggers inscription in the Registre National and generates the national identification number (matricule) — without it, CCSS, CNS, and tax registration are all blocked.
non_obvious_action_required: Book a commune appointment online or by phone before arrival. Bring the lease or employer accommodation letter, passport, employment contract, and passport photos. Do not wait — this step unlocks every downstream registration.
source: guichet.lu — Déclaration d'arrivée

step: Obtain certificat d'enregistrement (EU/EEA/Swiss nationals staying over 3 months)
field_label: Employment contract or proof of sufficient resources; health insurance; national ID
deadline_label: Within 3 months of arrival
source: guichet.lu — Certificat d'enregistrement pour citoyens UE/EEE/CH

step: Collect autorisation de séjour (residence permit card) from commune after arrival
authority: Direction de l'Immigration via administration communale
field_label: Approval decision letter; passport with visa D; biometric photos; proof of Luxembourg address
deadline_label: Within 90 days of entry on visa D
non_obvious_official_guidance: After the autorisation de séjour is approved, the employee enters Luxembourg on a long-stay visa D and must collect the physical residence permit card at the commune.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Many employees assume the approval letter is the permit. The physical card is mandatory for opening a bank account, CCSS registration, and other downstream steps. A separate commune appointment is required and card production takes several additional weeks.
non_obvious_action_required: Book the commune appointment immediately after arrival. Bring the approval decision, passport with visa D, passport photos, and proof of Luxembourg address. The card is the gating document for CCSS and banking — do not delay.
source: guichet.lu — Autorisation de séjour: salarié (ressortissant pays tiers)

step: Register employee with CCSS (Centre Commun de la Sécurité Sociale)
authority: Centre Commun de la Sécurité Sociale (CCSS)
field_label: Employee matricule (NIN); employment start date; gross salary; job category
deadline_label: Before or on first day of employment
non_obvious_official_guidance: Employers must declare every new employee to the CCSS before or on the first day of work via the CCSS online portal.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Luxembourg's CCSS covers five mandatory branches: pension, health, accident, dependency, and long-term care. Combined employer+employee contributions are among the highest in the EU (~25–27%). The employee has no direct registration action — it is entirely employer-initiated. If the commune declaration and NIN are delayed, CCSS registration is also blocked, preventing the legal employment start.
non_obvious_action_required: Ensure the employee's commune declaration and NIN are secured before the start date. Employer submits the déclaration d'entrée en service via ccss.public.lu. Retain the CCSS confirmation number — it is required for the CNS card and the tax fiche.
source: CCSS — Déclaration d'entrée et de sortie de service

step: Activate CNS health insurance card (Caisse Nationale de Santé)
field_label: CCSS affiliation confirmation; national ID number (matricule); CNS card request
deadline_label: Within first month of employment
source: CNS — Affiliés: affiliation et accès aux soins

step: Register with Administration des contributions directes and confirm tax class
form_name: Fiche de retenue d'impôt (tax withholding card) — employer requests via MyGuichet.lu
field_label: Tax class (1, 1a, or 2); number of dependants; marital status; resident or non-resident status
deadline_label: Before first payroll run
non_obvious_official_guidance: Luxembourg taxes employment income via monthly withholding (retenue d'impôt) based on the employee's tax class; the employer applies this via a fiche de retenue d'impôt issued by the ACD.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Three tax classes exist: Class 1 (single/no dependants, highest withholding), Class 1a (single parent or widowed), Class 2 (married/assimilated, most favourable). The tax class is not applied automatically — if no fiche is in place, the default Class 1 applies, often over-withholding significantly. Non-resident frontalier employees are withheld in Luxembourg but their final liability depends on a bilateral treaty and may require a return in both countries.
non_obvious_action_required: Employee provides personal status details; employer submits the fiche de retenue request via MyGuichet.lu before the first payroll. Non-resident employees should clarify their treaty position with the ACD or a cross-border tax adviser before month 1.
source: Administration des contributions directes — Retenue d'impôt sur les traitements et salaires

step: Obtain national identification number (matricule) via Registre National des Personnes Physiques
authority: Registre National des Personnes Physiques (RNPP) — via commune
field_label: 13-digit national number assigned automatically at commune registration
deadline_label: Issued automatically at commune déclaration d'arrivée
non_obvious_official_guidance: Luxembourg residents are assigned a 13-digit national identification number (matricule) when registered in the Registre National des Personnes Physiques, which happens at the commune declaration.
non_obvious_actual_reality: The matricule is required for every downstream step: CCSS, CNS, tax fiche, bank account, and the MyGuichet.lu digital portal. If the commune declaration is delayed for any reason, the entire administrative chain is blocked. EU/EEA nationals receive it as a separate document; TCNs find it on their residence permit card.
non_obvious_action_required: File the commune declaration on day 1 or 2 of arrival, not day 3. Ask the commune official explicitly to confirm the matricule number in writing. Share it with the employer's HR team immediately so CCSS and tax registration can proceed.
source: guichet.lu — Registre National des Personnes Physiques

step: Activate MyGuichet.lu account and obtain LuxTrust certificate for digital government services
authority: Centre des technologies de l'information de l'État (CTIE)
field_label: LuxTrust Scan token or compatible eIDAS credential; matricule number
deadline_label: Within first month — order LuxTrust before you need it
non_obvious_official_guidance: Residents access Luxembourg government services online via MyGuichet.lu using a LuxTrust certificate or compatible national eID.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Many downstream tasks (filing a tax return, tracking permit status, accessing CNS data) require a LuxTrust token which takes 7–14 days to arrive by post. LuxTrust is not free — the basic Scan token costs approximately €25/3 years. Employees who skip this step must attend in-person appointments for tasks that could be done online.
non_obvious_action_required: Order the LuxTrust certificate within the first week of arrival using the matricule number. Do not wait until a deadline is imminent — delivery delays are common.
source: guichet.lu — Se connecter à MyGuichet.lu

step: Open a Luxembourg bank account for salary receipt
authority: Commercial bank (regulated by Commission de Surveillance du Secteur Financier, CSSF)
field_label: Proof of Luxembourg address; employment contract; passport/ID; physical residence permit card (TCN)
deadline_label: Within first month — required for salary payment
non_obvious_official_guidance: EU residents have the right to a basic payment account under EU Directive 2014/92/EU.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Luxembourg banks apply stringent KYC checks due to the country's financial-centre status. TCN employees are frequently rejected or face extended delays without the physical residence permit card. Some Luxembourg employers will not pay salary to a non-LU IBAN, so a foreign fintech account may not bridge the gap.
non_obvious_action_required: Book a bank appointment as soon as the commune declaration is done (proof of address secured) and the residence permit card is collected. Bring originals, not copies. Confirm with the employer whether a foreign IBAN is accepted for the first payroll cycle.
source: CSSF — Accès au compte de paiement de base

step: File annual income tax return (déclaration pour l'impôt sur le revenu) — Modèle 100
field_label: World income; foreign income; deductible expenses; family charges; professional expenses
deadline_label: 31 March of the following year (extension to 31 December possible on request)
non_obvious_official_guidance: Resident taxpayers earning more than the non-taxable minimum or with multiple income sources must file an annual return.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Many Luxembourg salaried employees on Class 1 are over-withheld and entitled to a refund — but only if they file. Non-residents (frontaliers) must file in Luxembourg AND in their country of residence, applying bilateral treaty credits. Global income (foreign rental, dividends) must be declared and is frequently omitted.
non_obvious_action_required: File via MyGuichet.lu using LuxTrust credentials. Non-residents should engage a cross-border tax adviser to coordinate the dual declaration. File even when withholding appears correct — refunds are common, especially in the first partial year.
source: Administration des contributions directes — Déclaration pour l'impôt sur le revenu

step: Track physical presence against Luxembourg's 183-day tax residency threshold
field_label: Calendar days physically present in Luxembourg per tax year
deadline_label: Assessed annually (tax year = calendar year)
non_obvious_official_guidance: Luxembourg domestic law treats individuals as tax residents if they maintain a habitual abode or stay for more than 6 months (183 days) in Luxembourg in any calendar year.
non_obvious_actual_reality: For cross-border workers living in France, Belgium, or Germany, bilateral tax treaties contain their own tie-breaker rules that override the domestic 183-day threshold. Frontaliers are taxed primarily in Luxembourg regardless of day count, up to treaty-specific limits. This interaction is frequently misunderstood by employees who work partly from home in their country of residence.
non_obvious_action_required: If the employee lives outside Luxembourg and works partly from home, assess remote-work days against the applicable bilateral treaty before assuming Luxembourg-only withholding is correct. Consult a cross-border tax specialist for the first full tax year.
source: Administration des contributions directes — Résidence fiscale au Luxembourg

step: Assess permanent establishment (PE) and shadow payroll risk for hybrid/remote employees
field_label: Remote-work days in employee's country of residence; employer treaty position
deadline_label: Assessed from day 1 of any remote-work arrangement
non_obvious_official_guidance: If an employee regularly works from home in their country of residence, the employer may inadvertently create a taxable presence (permanent establishment) in that country, triggering corporate tax obligations there.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Luxembourg has specific bilateral agreements with Belgium, France, and Germany allowing tolerance thresholds of remote-work days per year before PE or additional social security obligations are triggered. Thresholds (e.g. ~34 days/year for Belgium; ~29 days/year for France under 2024 frameworks) are renegotiated periodically and are not published in Luxembourg domestic law, making them hard to track. Exceeding the threshold can create a shadow payroll obligation in the employee's country of residence.
non_obvious_action_required: Employer must track remote-work days by country for each cross-border employee from day 1. Implement a tracking policy before the employee starts. Engage a Luxembourg tax adviser to confirm current bilateral thresholds and set up shadow payroll if thresholds may be exceeded.
source: Administration des contributions directes — Frontaliers et télétravail

step: Obtain A1 certificate and determine applicable social security scheme under EU Regulation 883/2004
authority: Centre Commun de la Sécurité Sociale (CCSS)
form_name: A1 certificate (portable document confirming applicable legislation)
field_label: Country of social security registration; multi-state worker status; percentage of work performed in each country
deadline_label: Before or at employment start; reviewed annually for multi-state workers
non_obvious_official_guidance: Under EU Regulation 883/2004, a worker working in multiple EU member states may be subject to the legislation of the country where they perform a substantial part (≥25%) of their activity, or their country of residence.
non_obvious_actual_reality: For frontaliers working entirely in Luxembourg, Luxembourg social security applies without ambiguity. For employees who work partly from home in Belgium, France, or Germany: if home-country working days exceed 25% of total working time, social security shifts to the country of residence — requiring CCSS de-registration and re-registration abroad. Post-pandemic remote-work patterns have pushed many frontaliers over the 25% threshold unknowingly, creating retroactive dual-contribution exposure.
non_obvious_action_required: Employer must request the A1 certificate from CCSS for any multi-state worker. Monitor remote-work percentages annually. If the 25% threshold is approached, engage CCSS and a social security specialist to manage the potential transition.
source: CCSS — Travailleurs frontaliers et règlement EU 883/2004

step: Renew autorisation de séjour before expiry (third-country nationals)
form_name: Application for renewal of autorisation de séjour
field_label: Current permit expiry date; continued employment contract; CCSS affiliation proof
deadline_label: At least 2 months before permit expiry
non_obvious_official_guidance: Renewal applications must be submitted before the current authorisation expires. Working or remaining in Luxembourg after expiry without a valid permit is unlawful.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Initial authorisations are typically valid for 1–2 years matching the contract duration. Renewal is not automatic. If the renewal application is submitted before expiry, the employee may remain and work while it is processed (legal bridge). However, the physical card expires regardless — and banks and some services may refuse service on an expired card even when a renewal is pending.
non_obvious_action_required: Set a calendar reminder 3 months before expiry. Submit the renewal via MyGuichet.lu at least 2 months before expiry. Obtain a récépissé (receipt of application) from the commune to use as interim proof of legal status.
source: guichet.lu — Renouvellement de l'autorisation de séjour

step: Reassess tax class on life events (marriage, birth of child, change in spouse income)
form_name: Demande de changement de classe d'impôt
field_label: Marital status; spouse income; number of dependent children
deadline_label: Within the tax year in which the life event occurs
non_obvious_official_guidance: Employees may request a change of tax class from the ACD when a qualifying life event occurs (marriage, birth of child, spouse stops working).
non_obvious_actual_reality: Tax class changes are not applied automatically. An employee who marries and qualifies for Class 2 but does not submit the request continues to be withheld at Class 1 rates — potentially over-paying tax for an entire year. The ACD does not proactively notify employees of eligibility changes. For married non-residents, joint assessment rules under treaty may differ.
non_obvious_action_required: Request tax class change via MyGuichet.lu or by letter to the ACD immediately after the life event. For married non-residents, seek specialist advice on whether Class 2 applies given the bilateral treaty position.
source: Administration des contributions directes — Classes d'impôt

step: Monitor bilateral frontalier remote-work day thresholds (Belgium, France, Germany)
field_label: Remote-work days per country per calendar year; applicable bilateral agreement threshold
deadline_label: Monitored throughout tax year; assessed annually at year-end
non_obvious_official_guidance: Luxembourg has bilateral administrative agreements with Belgium, France, and Germany providing specific tolerances for cross-border remote work before additional tax or social security obligations are triggered in the country of residence.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Thresholds differ by country and are updated by negotiation: Belgium approximately 34 days/year of home working; France up to 29 days/year (2024 framework); Germany threshold was subject to ongoing bilateral discussions. These are administrative agreements, not domestic legislation — they can change without formal notice and are rarely publicised. Most frontalier employees and their HR teams are unaware until a cross-border tax audit surfaces the issue.
non_obvious_action_required: Employer implements a per-employee remote-work tracking policy from day 1. Review applicable thresholds annually via impotsdirects.public.lu. If thresholds may be exceeded, engage a cross-border tax specialist immediately — do not wait for year-end.
source: Administration des contributions directes — Télétravail et frontaliers
